title: SpaceX prices record $75 billion IPO at $135 per share before Nasdaq debut
summary: Reuters reported SpaceX priced a record $75 billion IPO at $135 per share, selling about 555.6 million shares at an implied valuation of roughly $1.77 trillion, with about 30% of the allocation reserved for retail investors. CNBC reported the Nasdaq debut was set for Friday, June 12 under ticker SPCX, while Bloomberg reported more than $70 billion of retail orders.
facts: Reuters reported SpaceX priced a record $75 billion IPO at $135 per share.
The offering size implies about 555.6 million shares sold.
Reuters put the implied valuation at roughly $1.77 trillion.
Reuters reported about 30% of the allocation was reserved for retail investors.
CNBC reported SpaceX was set to debut on Nasdaq on Friday, June 12 under ticker SPCX.
Bloomberg reported more than $70 billion of retail orders for the deal.

analysis.whatMoved: SpaceX converted one of the largest private-market valuation stories into a public IPO price, a trading date, and a stated allocation structure.
analysis.whyItMoved: The deal matters because a record $75 billion IPO at a roughly $1.77 trillion valuation creates a public benchmark for late-stage private marks, retail demand, and the IPO window for scaled technology issuers.
analysis.valuationImpact: The $135 per share IPO price gives the market a fresh observable mark. The first trading sessions will show whether investors accept that $1.77 trillion reference point or demand a discount after the scarcity premium is tested publicly.
analysis.financingImplication: A successful debut would tell bankers that very large IPO supply can clear when the issuer is scarce and demand is broad. Weak trading would warn other issuers that order-book size is not the same as durable aftermarket support.
analysis.sectorReadThrough: Read-through is strongest for late-stage venture-backed companies, defense and space infrastructure names, crossover funds, retail allocation strategies, and sponsors waiting for proof that the IPO window can absorb mega-cap private issuers.

parallel.precedent: Alibaba's 2014 IPO, Meta Platforms' 2012 IPO, and Arm's 2023 IPO are useful large technology debut comparisons because each became a benchmark for investor appetite beyond its own company.
parallel.outcome: Those deals showed that large IPOs can clear when the issuer is high quality, but the lasting read depends on aftermarket trading, lock-up supply, profitability, and whether the next issuers share similar scarcity value.
parallel.whatRhymes: SpaceX similarly gives bankers and investors a headline valuation, a public trading reference, and a demand signal that can influence other IPO candidates.
parallel.whatDiffers: SpaceX has a unique mix of launch, satellite, communications, and defense-adjacent exposure, so its IPO may say more about scarce strategic assets than about every late-stage technology company.
parallel.soWhat: Treat the debut as a powerful benchmark, but separate a one-company scarcity trade from a broad reopening of the IPO market.

analysis.watchNext: Watch the opening print, first-day close versus $135, stabilization activity, allocation disclosures, lock-up details, and whether other late-stage issuers accelerate filing plans after the SpaceX debut.
